summary: This document defines syntax for two Cryptographic Message Syntax content types, a key package receipt and a key package error. The receipt confirms that an identified key package was received, and the error reports a problem.

plainLanguage.summary: When you send a locked box of keys, you want a receipt saying it arrived or a note saying why it did not. This defines both notes.

subtitle: Two CMS message types that let a key package receiver say it arrived, or say exactly why it was rejected.

tldr.problem: When keying material is sent in key packages, the sender needs a signed confirmation that a package arrived, or a clear reason it was rejected.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a key package receipt content type, a key package error content type with enumerated error codes, a receipt-request attribute, and a name format for the entities involved.
tldr.outcome: Both content types are DER encoded and are normally wrapped in CMS signing and optionally encryption, so senders can confirm delivery and diagnose failures.

today: RFC 7191 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Receipts and Errors for Key Packages
sections.content:
This document defines two Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) content types. The key package receipt confirms receipt of an identified key package or collection of key packages. The key package error says an error occurred while processing one. CMS can digitally sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt either of them.

A package for which a receipt is generated MUST be signed, and it MUST include the key-package-identifier-and-receipt-request attribute. A package for which an error is generated might be signed, and may be identified by the same attribute. The syntax is written in ASN.1.
sections.plainLanguage: It defines two kinds of notes for a key delivery: one that says it arrived and one that says what went wrong.

sections.title: SIR Entity Names
sections.content:
Within a key distribution system, sources, intermediaries and receivers are identified by a Source Intermediary Recipient (SIR) entity name. It has a nameType object identifier and a nameValue octet string. The type prevents two identifiers of different kinds that happen to hold the same bytes from being treated as equal. Two names of the same type are equal if their octet strings are the same length and contain the same octets.

One type is defined here: the DN type, which carries an X.509 Distinguished Name. Other types can be registered, for example for an organization or for a specific device, and using object identifiers avoids a central registry of name types.
sections.plainLanguage: Every sender and receiver gets a name tag. The tag also says what kind of name it is, so a person's name is never mixed up with a serial number.

sections.title: The Receipt Request Attribute
sections.content:
The key-package-identifier-and-receipt-request attribute lets the originator identify a package and optionally ask for receipts. It can appear as a signed, authenticated or content attribute, and it MUST have exactly one attribute value.

It contains a pkgID (an octet string with no imposed structure) and an optional receiptReq. The request holds an encryptReceipt flag (if set, the receipt SHOULD be encrypted), an optional receiptsFrom list and a required receiptsTo list. If receiptsFrom is absent, all receivers are expected to return receipts. If present, a receiver SHOULD return one only if its SIR entity name is listed. A receiver SHOULD ignore any unrecognized name type.

If the attribute appears in more than one place in a package, each occurrence is evaluated independently, so a receiver may generate more than one receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender writes on the box: here is my box number, please tell these people it arrived, and send the note to this address.

sections.title: The Key Package Receipt
sections.content:
A KeyPackageReceipt has a version (default v2, which MUST be used; v1 is deprecated), receiptOf and receivedBy. The receiptOf field identifies the package, either by pkgID (which MUST be supported and MUST exactly match the identifier in the request attribute) or by an alternate attribute. receivedBy is the SIR entity name of the receiver. The content type MUST be DER encoded.

A receipt MUST be encapsulated in a CMS SignedData, and MAY also be encrypted with EncryptedData, EnvelopedData or AuthEnvelopedData. If both are used, it MUST be signed before it is encrypted. If the signer has a real-time clock, the binary-signing-time attribute SHOULD be included.

Delivery assurance remains the job of the protocol that transports and tracks key packages. The receipt is one piece of such a solution.
sections.plainLanguage: The receipt says which box arrived and who got it, and it is signed so nobody can fake it.

sections.title: The Key Package Error
sections.content:
A KeyPackageError has a version (again v2 by default), an optional errorOf identifier, an errorBy SIR entity name and an errorCode. The errorOf field is left out when the receiver or intermediary cannot parse the data to find the identifier, or when encryption hides it. The content type MUST be DER encoded.

The error code is either an enumerated code or an object identifier. The enumerated form MUST be supported; the object identifier form MAY be. The codes cover problems such as decodeFailure (1), badSignedData (3), noTrustAnchor (10), notAuthorized (11), signatureFailure (16), incorrectTarget (23), missingSignature (29), revokedCertificate (33), noDecryptKey (61), decryptFailure (71) and other (127). Values up to 33 are aligned with RFC 5934, and the list is expected to grow.
sections.plainLanguage: If the box cannot be used, the error note says why, such as the lock being broken, the signature not matching, or the box going to the wrong person.

sections.title: Protection and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Receipts and errors are not necessarily protected by themselves. CMS can protect them with SignedData for a signature, EncryptedData or EnvelopedData for encryption, AuthenticatedData for integrity, or AuthEnvelopedData for authenticated encryption. The media type for carrying them is specified in RFC 7193.

The receipt request lists have no size limit, and the receiptsTo entries need not relate to the sender. To avoid denial-of-service amplification, receipts should only be returned for key packages with a valid signature from a trusted signer.

If several sources are accepted, the same key package identifier could be used by more than one, and receipts could be confused. A convention for assigning identifiers avoids this. Very detailed errors can help an attacker, so where that matters an implementation should return the most generic suitable error code, and may allow configuring generic or detailed codes.
sections.plainLanguage: A note can be forged or misused, so only answer boxes that are properly signed, and do not give away too many clues in the error notes.
